newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGBs seen ignoring corporate bond stampede.
newsitem.headline: JGBs seen ignoring corporate bond stampede.

text.p: Yields of Japanese government bonds are likely to keep falling despite a recent barrage of corporate bond launches, traders and analysts say.

According to the Bond Underwriters Association of Japan, 603 billion yen worth of corporate straight bonds were launched from April 7 to April 15, more than four times the amount launched in all of March.

But the recent demand-driven strength in the JGB market is unlikely to change despite the flood of new corporate bonds, said Masuhisa Kobayashi, vice-president and fixed income analyst at Merrill Lynch & Co in Japan.

"New money has flowed into JGBs since the start of the new business year on April 1, and a large amount of JGBs, about five to six trillion yen worth, will come due around June, so the supply-and-demand balance as a whole is still very tight and I do not think the rush of corporate bonds is making JGBs heavy on the upside," Kobayashi said.
Bond traders said that recently launched corporate bonds, such as those issued by electric power companies, have not met with enthusiastic investor demand so far.

Some bond underwriters have struggled to sell bonds launched by Hokuriku Electric Power Co Inc and Chubu Electric Power Co Inc and the bonds are now being offered in the secondary market at well below their issue prices, a senior trader for a city bank's securities unit said.
But the fall in corporate bond prices was seen reflecting the temporary effects of the onrush of new issues or coupon rates that were set too low.

Investors are willing to buy corporate bonds as long as the terms are right, but they are avoiding corporate bonds whose yield spreads from JGBs are too thin, said Tatsuhiko Takeda, deputy manager at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd's bond sales promotion department.

The fact that Nomura Securities Co Ltd has not been invited to join syndication groups since it came under suspicion of involvement in illegal deals may also be contributing to sluggish sales of corporate bonds, Takeda said.

On March 6, Nomura announced that an internal probe had found that two of its directors had been involved in apparently illegal deals which involved transferring money from a Nomura account to a corporate client's account.

But bonds are still the investment vehicle of choice for investors and JGBs may make a try for record highs once the current wave of bond launches passes, said Yasunari Ueno, chief market economist of Fuji Securities Co Ltd's research group.

"There is still uncertainty about the strength of the economic recovery and there are lingering worries about the financial system and weakness of share prices. Investor demand for cash JGBs has not waned. Against this backdrop, I think JGBs may make a try for new highs in May," Ueno said.

Electric power companies, which accounted for about 25 percent of the corporate bonds issued in 1996, are planning to cut back the annual amount of bond issues from the previous year, so the over-supply of corporate bonds is unlikely to persist over the long term, Ueno added.
The yield of the benchmark 182nd 10-year JGB ended Tokyo trade on Wednesday at 2.150 percent." -- Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-3-5473-3748
